Its early form had a wooden body, a slender fretted neck and three strings, and the body could be round, hexagonal or octagonal, the hexagonal one with rounded edges also called the plum-blossom qin. It is popular in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau and is used in Guangdong music, Chaozhou music and Hakka Han music; some local silk-and-bamboo bands often use only two strings. In Taiwan it also appears in Beiguan, gezaixi opera and glove puppetry. The two-string đàn sến of Vietnamese traditional music was adapted from it. The qin qin (Qin Qin) is a traditional Chinese plucked instrument of the folk repertoire and a chordophone. It is built from a wooden soundbox, neck and tuning pegs, and the soundbox may be round, hexagonal or octagonal, the hexagonal one also called the plum-blossom qin; it usually has three strings, and two are also found. Modern versions mostly have a round soundbox covered with sheepskin or python skin and look like a banjo. It is played by plucking with the fingers; the frets stand high, so the fingertips do not touch the soundboard, which helps control the timbre and intonation but makes chords harder to stop. The qin qin is popular in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau and is used in Guangdong music, Chaozhou music and Hakka Han music; Taiwan's Beiguan, gezaixi opera and glove puppetry also use it. Traditional music in southern Vietnam also has the two-string đàn sến that developed from the qin qin.

The qin qin is good at flowing melodic lines and can also carry rhythmic accompaniment, and in an ensemble it blends naturally into the overall sound while keeping its part clearly identifiable.
